content: Obstructive lung disease refers to a group of conditions characterized by structural abnormalities that lead to the narrowing or collapse of the airways. Patients with obstructive lung disease often experience shortness of breath, which is primarily caused by damage to the airways within the lungs. This damage impairs the ability to fully exhale air, resulting in an abnormally high volume of air remaining in the lungs after maximal expiration. These substances include cigarette smoke, air pollution, chemical fumes, and dust. In the early stages of the disease, patients are often asymptomatic. However, as the disease progresses, symptoms become more pronounced. Common symptoms include a productive cough, difficulty breathing, wheezing, and a sensation of chest tightness. Diseases that fall under the category of obstructive lung disease include asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), bronchiolitis, bronchiectasis, heart failure, tuberculosis, cystic fibrosis, and lymphangioleiomyomatosis. Pulmonary function tests in these conditions typically reveal an obstructive pattern, which is characterized by an increase in total lung capacity (TLC) and residual volume (RV), along with a decrease in forced vital capacity (FVC), forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1), and the FEV1/FVC ratio. The classification of obstructive lung diseases includes the following conditions: Asthma Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) Bronchiolitis Bronchiectasis Heart failure Tuberculosis Lymphangioleiomyomatosis Cystic fibrosis Spirometry is a valuable diagnostic tool for distinguishing obstructive lung disease from restrictive lung disease. In obstructive lung disease, spirometry findings typically show reduced airflow during expiration, which is reflected in a decreased FEV1 and FEV1/FVC ratio. This pattern helps differentiate obstructive lung diseases from other pulmonary conditions. To differentiate between various diseases that present with an obstructive pattern on pulmonary function tests, a detailed clinical evaluation, along with specific diagnostic tests, is required. Each condition has unique clinical features, imaging findings, and laboratory results that aid in making an accurate diagnosis.
